title: Shiva's drum and the sacred sounds
hook: at the end of Shiva's dance his drum sounds fourteen times, and a grammarian hears the alphabet
carry: the sound itself is sacred: shiva's drum
tomorrow: why was baby Krishna named in secret?

segments.voice: Yesterday, nama japa: a robber changed by Rama's name, even said backwards, and matra, the long ā where the voice rests. Today, the other side of it: why the sounds themselves matter.

Picture Shiva as Nataraja, the dancer, ringed in flame. In one of his upper hands is a small drum shaped like an hourglass, the damaru. Grammarians tell a story about it. At the end of his dance, Shiva struck the drum fourteen times. And Panini, the great grammarian of Sanskrit, heard in those fourteen beats fourteen short lines of sounds, and made them the key to his whole grammar.

Those fourteen lines are still called the Shiva Sutras, and they open Panini's grammar. Whatever you make of the story, the teaching inside it is very Hindu: sound is sacred. In Nataraja's hand, the drum is commonly read as creation, the first sound from which the world unfolds, with the fire in another hand as its ending. The Vedas are called shruti, what was heard. For many centuries they were passed mouth to ear, teacher to student, and reciters guarded every sound so carefully that the chants came down remarkably intact. That's why a grandmother corrects a syllable. Not because God can't understand you, but because the sound is part of the offering. And it's why the alphabet is laid out like a map of the mouth. The first row of consonants is made at the back, in the throat: ka, kha, ga, gha, nga. The next at the palate: cha, chha, ja, jha, nya. Then a row at the roof of the mouth, for tomorrow. Then the teeth: ta, tha, da, dha, na. Last, the lips: pa, pha, ba, bha, ma. Say ka, cha, ta, pa, and the sound walks forward out of you. The map even solves a puzzle on the page: in careful spelling, c is always said ch. Cakra is chakra. Candra, the moon, is chandra. Yesterday said the name works even said wrong. Today adds the other half: saying it with care is a way of loving it.
screen: `THE SHIVA SUTRAS.` · `SHRUTI: WHAT WAS HEARD.` · `THE SOUND IS PART OF THE OFFERING.` · `THROAT, PALATE, ROOF, TEETH, LIPS.` · then, large: `CARE IS A WAY OF LOVING IT.`

segments.voice: One out-breath at a time, say slowly: ka, at the back of the throat; cha, the middle of the tongue rising; ta, at the teeth; pa, at the lips. Rest a breath, then walk the sounds forward again. If you pray, end with a mantra you know, each sound placed with care; if not, end with ma and let it fade into the breath.
Ka. The first consonant, made in the throat, where the map of the mouth begins: throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips.
Your line: the sound itself is sacred, Shiva's drum. Tomorrow: why was baby Krishna named in secret? Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus treat sacred sound with care: the Vedas were passed mouth to ear for centuries, mantras are learned from a teacher syllable by syllable, and students recite the consonants row by row from the throat to the lips; tradition says the fourteen Shiva Sutras that open Panini's grammar sounded from Nataraja's drum.
